research.abstract: ABSTRACT The architecture of gene-expression variation and its relationship to population differentiation remain incompletely characterized in crops. Subpopulation identity explained a mean of 5.3% of expression variation across genes, indicating that most expression diversity segregates within rather than among breeding populations. We identified 17,468 genes with cis -eQTLs and resolved putatively causal eQTLs for 16,270 of them. Most fine-mapped eGenes (77.7%) were haplotype-rich (at least two credible sets), and approximately 39% of credible sets contained a single variant. Modeling all credible sets increased median R 2 from 0.16 to 0.27. Individual effects were generally modest, and genes with more signals tended to have higher expression heritability. Fine-mapped variants were enriched in transcribed regions, accessible chromatin, and transcription-factor-binding regions, with the latter enrichment persisting after accessibility matching. Genes with high gene-body sequence constraint had modestly smaller regulatory effects and fewer credible sets. Across five population contrasts, including Stiff Stalk–Non-Stiff Stalk comparisons within two breeding eras, genes with stronger statistical evidence of differential expression were associated with higher F ST at fine-mapped variants. These results indicate that single-variant summaries provide an incomplete picture of cis -regulatory loci, and offer a mechanism for why transcriptome-wide association studies identify genes missed by genome-wide association studies in the same populations.

research.abstract: Abstract Climate change is profoundly affecting species worldwide and poses a major threat to their long-term persistence. Although trees may have the potential for rapid adaptation to changing climates, empirical evidence remains limited, and whether these long-lived organisms can adapt quickly enough to keep pace with ongoing climate change is still an open question. To investigate real-time responses to contemporary climate change, we combined genomic data from 82 range-wide populations of the widespread tree Pinus pinaster Ait. with intensive sampling of two successive cohorts from two natural populations. Using an original genotype-environment association (GEA) approach to quantify climate (mal)adaptation, we found that most individuals from both target populations showed evidence of an adaptive lag to current climatic conditions, and are predicted to face substantial risk of maladaptation under future climates. Importantly, changes in genomic composition at climate-associated loci between cohorts were consistent with rapid evolutionary responses to ongoing climate change and could not be explained by neutral demographic processes alone, as supported by forward-time genetic simulations. We also observed a lower realised genetic load in the younger cohort, suggesting that the dynamics of deleterious mutations may change with climatic pressure. Our work provides evidence suggesting genetic responses to contemporary climate change within a single generation, including signals of rapid evolutionary changes in genomic composition at climate-associated loci and signatures of purifying selection, despite widespread adaptive lag to current climates. These findings challenge the view that trees only respond slowly to environmental change and highlight the need to integrate evolutionary dynamics into predictive models of species persistence under future climates.

research.abstract: Abstract Although steroidal saponins from Dioscorea species have substantial economic value and versatile utilization potential, the evolutionary origin and regulatory mechanisms underlying their biosynthesis remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comparative genomic analysis across representative plant lineages ranging from algae to angiosperms to examine the copy number variation and syntenic organization of steroidal saponin biosynthetic genes. Our results reveal that ancestral sterol biosynthetic components were already present in bryophytes. However, synteny analysis indicates that stable genomic integration of these genes was established no earlier than in pteridophytes. By integrating transcriptome–metabolome association analyses with branch-site selection tests, we identified strong positive selection acting on DcWRKY33 within the Dioscorea lineage, suggesting adaptive evolution and highlighting the importance of regulatory innovation in steroidal saponin diversification. Functional analyses demonstrated that DcWRKY33 functions as a positive regulator of steroidal saponin biosynthesis: transient overexpression upregulates the expression of structural genes and increases saponin accumulation, whereas gene silencing produced opposite effects. Mechanistically, dual-luciferase and yeast one-hybrid assays indicated that DcWRKY33 activates DcHDR and DcCYP51, while indirectly regulating DcHMGR through modulation of DcWRKY11, thereby orchestrating biosynthesis across both the MEP and MVA pathways. Promoter analysis revealed W-box motifs partially absence in non-saponin-producing Dioscorea, and heterologous expression in tobacco confirmed lineage-specific regulatory capacity despite conserved cis-elements. Collectively, our study links pathway evolution with regulatory innovation and establishes a mechanistic framework for understanding the evolution and transcriptional control of steroidal saponin biosynthesis in D. composita, providing insights for metabolic improvement of medicinal and horticultural yam species.

research.abstract: Abstract Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) can arise early in the development of aggressive tumors or later upon progression, but the impact of chronology on patient outcome is not known. Currently, it is not possible to determine when an ecDNA arose in the course of tumor development and progression, based on genome sequencing data. Here, we develop an analytic method, ecEvol, to infer ecDNA emergence time, selection strength, mutation rate, and clonal dominance from allele-frequency spectra in bulk whole-genome sequencing. EcEvol outperforms other methods and predicts parameters with high accuracy across a wide range of parameter values. Applying ecEvol to primary, treatment-naive tumors, we find that ecDNA typically emerges early and undergoes strong positive selection, albeit with substantial variation across cancer types. EcDNAs carrying known oncogenes emerge earlier and reach greater clonal dominance than ecDNAs lacking known oncogenes. In advanced and predominantly treated tumors, ecDNA emerges substantially later than in matched primary tumors, consistent with the generation and selection of new ecDNA during tumor progression and therapy. Longitudinal samples further support continued expansion of ecDNA-bearing lineages. Finally, earlier ecDNA emergence is associated with poorer overall survival. These results provide insight into the chronology of ecDNA formation from a single tumor biopsy taken at any point during the course of the disease, revealing that allele-frequency spectra encode the evolutionary history of ecDNA and provide a quantitative framework for reconstructing its emergence and expansion.

research.abstract: Abstract Ion channels regulate cell proliferation, survival and migration, but the functional consequences of many ion channel mutations in cancer are unknown, and electrophysiological characterisation at scale is impractical. Here we use the mutational landscape of colorectal adenocarcinoma as a functional filter to identify potassium channel mutations under selection. A dN/dS screen of 16 potassium channels expressed in the large intestine identified KCNA5 (Kv1.5) as the strongest candidate under positive mutational selection. These mutations cluster in the T1 tetramerisation, S1–S4 voltage-sensor and pore domains, yet avoid the selectivity filter, indicating that selection does not favour loss of conduction. Within the pore region, the observed mutations occupy a biophysical space distinct from known C-type inactivation, activation-gate and toxin-binding mutations. In the voltage sensor, mutations affect gating-charge arginines. In the T1 domain, mutations fall on inter-subunit interfaces conserved across the KCNA family, and saturation mutagenesis energy calculations predict that they destabilise subunit contacts or the folding of the domain. Molecular dynamics simulations of D166N and G128R show loss of coordinated interface dynamics and distortion of the local backbone, respectively. Transcriptomic analysis of KCNA5-mutant tumours shows reduced expression of cell-cycle, KRAS-related and inflammatory pathways, and we observe differences between transcriptional effects induced by T1 and S1-S4 domain mutations. These changes are not reproduced by low KCNA5 expression alone, consistent with an effect specific to the mutant protein. Together, these computational results highlight that KCNA5 is under mutational selection in colorectal adenocarcinoma, and that these mutations are likely functional and induce phenotypic effects on tumors.

We develop a new approach, the tissue time machine , applied to predict outcomes of non-human primate granulomas from initiation to endpoint using single timepoint tissue datasets including high-dimensional spatial features. This involves identifying granuloma digital partners , simulations most closely resembling real granulomas from a virtual library of over 50,000. By analyzing digital partners, we predict infection outcomes of 22/28 granulomas, and that Mtb-specific, IFN-γ-producing T cell recruitment rates influence uncertainty for the 6/28. This method is applicable to any system that allows for mechanistic predictions over time using heterogeneous, incomplete, and high-dimensional datasets.

Here, we develop GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function), a framework that trains supervised classifiers on multimodal variant effect predictions (ATAC-seq and RNA-seq) from the sequence-to-function model Borzoi and applies SHAP-based attribution to associate individual GWAS variants with the cell types most relevant to their disease association. Applied to asthma, LDL cholesterol, multiple sclerosis, and type 2 diabetes, GEMS prioritizes known disease-relevant cell types concordant with stratified LD-score regression. At the variant level, GEMS associates a median of 58.7% of fine-mapped variants with at least one cell type via ATAC-seq and 65.9% via RNA-seq, extending cellular annotation beyond the chromatin accessibility peaks in the single-cell atlas used for model training. ATAC-seq variant–cell-type associations are significantly enriched in cis-regulatory elements from independent experimental studies not used in model training, and enrichment persists after excluding variants overlapping training atlas peaks. For multiple sclerosis, hierarchical biclustering of variant–cell-type associations partitions risk variants into immune and CNS modules driven by distinct transcription factor families, recapitulating the immune-mediated and neurodegenerative components of the disease and demonstrating that integrative analysis of sequence-to-function predictions can stratify phenotype-associated variants into mechanistically distinct, cell-type-specific regulatory programs.

research.abstract: Abstract Codon substitution models detect natural selection by comparing non-synonymous ( dN ) and synonymous ( dS ) rates at each site. Standard methods assume stationary nucleotide composition across the phylogeny. In many genomes, however, GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC), codon usage bias, strand asymmetry, and host deaminases drive directional shifts in base composition along lineages. Under a stationary Muse–Gaut model with site-to-site synonymous rate variation ( FEL ), position-specific base frequencies and site-specific dS absorb most tree-wide drift. As a result, selection calls remain unchanged at 96%–99% of codons. At the remaining boundary sites, however, directional shifts bias dS in opposite directions depending on the ancestral codon. Rapid silent turnover at codons shifting toward the favored base inflates dS , producing apparent purifying selection and increasing across-site synonymous rate variance. Conversely, when amino acid replacements oppose the compositional tide, stationary models miss diversifying selection. Branch-specific models can accommodate shifting base frequencies, but diagonalizing a separate non-reversible codon rate matrix on every branch is too slow for large trees. Here we introduce Directional Fixed Effects Likelihood ( dFEL ). The method first tests whether base composition varies across taxa and runs standard FEL when frequencies are uniform. When composition shifts across lineages, dFEL roots the tree by maximum likelihood without an outgroup and models each branch as a smooth weighted average of three regime-specific transition probability matrices representing AT-enriching, neutral, and GC-enriching evolution. Sharing these matrices across the tree requires only three matrix diagonalizations per site. We validate dFEL across 1,800 simulated alignments and 87 unique empirical alignments (93 benchmark analyses) spanning up to 869 vertebrate species. It maintains calibrated false-positive rates, improves power, cuts whole-gene synonymous rate variance by up to 63%, and recovers established roots from coding sequences alone ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ).
